migration.migration_reason: Legacy support adjudication is derived deterministically from the already current-validator-approved canonical owner records. No new model judgment or score is introduced.

C++.justification: `int parse_twice(const std::string& s){ return std::stoi(s)*2; }` — std::stoi throws std::invalid_argument/std::out_of_range on failure; unhandled, it propagates automatically to the caller.

Go.justification: func parse_twice(s string) (int, error) { n, err := strconv.Atoi(s); if err != nil { return 0, err }; return n*2, nil } -- idiomatic explicit error propagation, visible in the declared (int, error) signature.

Java.fragment: static int parseTwice(String s) { return Integer.parseInt(s) * 2; }
Java.justification: int parse_twice(String s) { return Integer.parseInt(s) * 2; } — Integer.parseInt throws unchecked NumberFormatException which propagates automatically without explicit handling.

Kotlin.justification: fun parseTwice(s: String): Int { val n = s.toInt(); return n * 2 } — toInt() throws NumberFormatException on failure and propagates unhandled (Kotlin/JVM has no checked exceptions, so this is the normal propagation mechanism).

Python.justification: int(s) raises ValueError on malformed input and propagates unhandled by Python's default exception-propagation semantics; no special declaration syntax is required or omitted.

Quidra.citation: language.md 'Error propagation and match': `int | error` return type plus `try` propagation is exactly this pattern; llm-guide.md complete example mirrors it directly.
Quidra.fragment:
int | error parse_twice(string s)
    int value = try int.parse(s)
    return value * 2
Quidra.justification: language.md 'Error propagation and match': `int | error` return type plus `try` propagation is exactly this pattern; llm-guide.md complete example mirrors it directly.

Rust.fragment: fn parse_twice(s: &str) -> Result<i32, std::num::ParseIntError> { let v: i32 = s.parse()?; Ok(v * 2) }

Swift.justification: func parse_twice(_ s: String) throws -> Int32 { guard let v = Int32(s) else { throw ParseError.invalid }; return v * 2 } — throws in the declared signature and propagation via throw is Swift's normal, visible mechanism.

TypeScript.justification: The standard Number/parseInt conversions report malformed input as NaN rather than a propagating failure. Adding an isNaN check handles and manufactures the failure locally, contrary to the canonical requirement to propagate the standard conversion's own failure without handling it. F13.P1 has no R9 substitution.

Zig.fragment: fn parse_twice(s: []const u8) !i32 { const v = try std.fmt.parseInt(i32, s, 10); return v * 2; }
Zig.justification: std.fmt.parseInt returns an error union (![]u8->!i32); `try` propagates the failure to the caller, and the function's own return type (!i32) documents fallibility.
